P1.evidence: Nothing from the setter was read back — the rep did not know the prospect's occupation and said so 53 minutes in: 'What did you say you did for work again? I can't remember. I don't know if we talked about it.' The frame was three parts plus next steps: 'figure out where you're at in your fitness journey, like where we're at right now, where we're trying to get to, what's missing. And then from there, we can kind of create a game plan and talk about some potential next steps.' Frame agreement taken — 'Does that all sound good to you?' — and the open question ran: 'what are you potentially hoping that we could help you with?'

P2.evidence: Age, height and weight were asked. Training week and a full day of eating were asked and answered in detail. Everything safety-relevant was missed. Health conditions were never asked — the diabetes diagnosis, the declined metformin, the nutritionist's carb ceiling and the sleep apnoea were all volunteered inside other answers. Injuries and movement limitations were never asked — the back pain and 'I cannot do a squat in self-defense, I lift my heels' surfaced only because the prospect narrated his own workout. Sleep was never asked despite a CPAP and a collapse from nearly eight hours to six. Work was asked at the end and only as small talk, so the fact that he lifts print material all day never entered the picture.

P3.evidence: The goal question was asked at the outcome level rather than the one-thing level: 'What's the ultimate goal with our fitness?' The why-bridge ran well — 'why are you feeling like it is so important for you to get in the shape that we're talking about' — and produced the hiking, the photography and the loss of his partner. The reflect-back was accurate and the prospect confirmed it: 'this comes down to, hey, there's going to be a lot of pain and hurt, and we need somewhere to channel the energy and something productive to do rather than just spiral.' — 'Yes, exactly.' Never asked what one thing he would change, never asked what he wants to do physically but cannot (the squat and pull-up were volunteered), and never asked who else this impacts.

P4.evidence: No past-attempts question at all. What emerged came from the prospect's own narration of the diabetes years — 'I was hitting it hard, but I was not seeing any changes.' The gap question ran and worked: 'what do you feel is missing? Like, what do we need to fill in for you to get you to that shape?' produced the cleanest self-diagnosis in the batch — 'A process... I'm bouncing back and forth and I'm doing what I like instead of what I need.' The 'information isn't the problem, why can't you stick to it on your own' challenge was never put, which matters because this prospect has a nutritionist, an app and a tracked deficit — his adherence is demonstrably fine and the actual gap is programme design.

P5.evidence: Run properly and then run again when the first answer drifted into history: 'what is the next two years, three years look like for you if we don't go down this path?' and then 'what do you feel like the next couple of years would be like emotionally for you if we don't do something like this?' That second question produced the most valuable material on the call — 'my worst fear is that I will give up. I will, what's the point, I'm already 60.' The rep then left it there. No 'is that something you're willing to settle for', no 'why not', no line in the sand, so the fear was surfaced and never converted.

P6.evidence: The go-all-in question ran close to script: 'provided we can actually work out the logistics, Juan, are you really in a point where you really want to commit to something like this?' The answer was explicitly conditional — 'I will do whatever it takes there in my range of possibility right now that I'm totally, it's an unknown what's going to happen' — and the rep treated it as a yes and moved to price. The check exists to stop exactly that. The belief question was replaced by a product-fit question: 'Do you feel like that's everything that you need to get into like the best shape you've ever been in as a 60 year old?'

P11.evidence: A close was attempted and no payment was collected, so step 1 is a miss and steps 2-4 were unreachable. The only thing sent was a third-party financing application the prospect did not complete on the call. No onboarding booked, no agreement, no follow-up date.

objection_plays.detail: Isolation ran twice and correctly: 'finances aside, is there, like, are we feeling 100% like this is the right thing, now is the right time?' followed by 'why are we feeling that way?', then the should-versus-how reframe almost verbatim: 'we're not in a should-a-do-it place where we're going back and forth on if it's the right thing. Right now, it's more like a how do we do it.' Of the six financial-picture questions, two ran — 'what's actually even accessible in that right now?' (answer: nothing, the account is negative) and credit score, which is not a scripted move. No cards, no available credit, no used-versus-available, no investments. The break-it-up move was never made: the prospect proposed roughly $1,000 a month himself and the rep neither accepted, countered nor quoted anything, deflecting instead to 'bean counters' and a financing link. The play answered the question of whether he could pay with a clear no, and the close continued anyway.

Trigger was explicit — 'six grand right now is a no-go right now because of the way that it is' and 'maybe it's not the right time. Maybe when I less stressed out.' The rep ran an inverted urgency argument rather than the scripted moves: 'situations only going to get worse financially as things go on, and we're in the best situation we can be right now.' None of 'things never slow down', 'when does it actually become the right time', 'the longer you wait the harder this gets', or 'what if all you had to do was show up and everything else was handled' were used — and the last of those was the strongest available line for a man whose stated gap is that he cannot design his own programme.

'I'm going to have to think about it. It's not something that I can just say like in the, oh. A hundred bucks a week. Let's go for it.' Not one move from the play was run — no 'do you feel what we've gone through can get you there', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'what's actually coming up that's preventing you from getting started'. The rep went straight to a financial probe instead, which was arguably the right instinct given what he already knew, but the play was left on the table.

Script gap — a competing spend that is not a cheaper substitute but a different category of need. The prospect put marriage counselling on the table as the thing that might consume the same money: 'even with insurance, it makes Trevor's investments none... now I'm down for way above six grand, just with the shrink to try to make it work.' There is no scripted path for this and the improvisation was to undercut the competing spend — 'even if you guys do end up doing therapy, that's still not guarantee of a positive outcome in the marriage.' Flagged separately on conduct. The script needs a defined position on prospects choosing between the programme and a clinical or therapeutic service.

Script gap — a prospect whose finances are frozen by a live legal process rather than merely tight. The joint account is inaccessible, the personal account is overdrawn, and any charge is expected to become contested: 'a week later, I'm going to have her screaming and yelling, just put it in your credit card, $6,000, and it's just going to create already chaos in super chaos.' OC has no branch for money that exists but cannot lawfully or safely be spent, and the fallback of consumer credit makes the situation worse rather than better.

notes: The consequence frame was the best-run version of P5 in this batch and the rep still walked away from what it produced. The structural failure is P2: a diabetic on a CPAP who cannot squat unassisted was taken through a full presentation without one health, injury or sleep question, so the nutrition pillar was pitched straight across a plan his physician and nutritionist had built. Second coaching point: once the financial picture returned an overdrawn account and a struggling car payment, the correct move was to disqualify or defer, not to escalate to consumer credit.
